title: Trap Muzik

paras: Arista dropped T.I. after his 2001 debut I’m Serious; what he built next — his own label Grand Hustle, a partnership with producer DJ Toomp, and a word for the music that hadn’t existed as a genre yet — became Trap Muzik, released 19 August 2003, which debuted at No. 4 on the Billboard 200 on 110,000 copies in its first week and went Platinum. It gave the trap its name, not as a marketing term but as a place T.I. described in the first person, with the boredom and the arithmetic left in.

Almost all of it was made here. Between March and May of 2003 the record went from beats on a hard drive to a sequenced album in a ten-week sprint across three Patchwerk rooms, frequently two at once — vocals in 995 while Leslie Brathwaite mixed in 9000.

items.a: T.I. recorded Trap Muzik at Patchwerk Recording Studios in Atlanta, Georgia. Patchwerk’s own daily session reports document 48 sessions for the album between March 2002 and December 2003, spread across Studio 995, Studio 9000 and the dub room at 1094 Hemphill Avenue. Most of the record was finished in a ten-week run from March to May 2003, often with two rooms working the same night.

Leslie Brathwaite mixed Trap Muzik at Patchwerk Recording Studios, and Mark “Exit” Goodchild, Steve Fisher, Mike Wilson and Ismel Ramos engineered the tracking sessions. Cory Williams, Mike Davis and Howard White assisted. Brathwaite mixed the title track, “T.I. vs T.I.P.” and “Let’s Get Away” in Studio 9000; Exit cut vocals on “Let’s Get Away,” “Rubber Band Man” and “Doin’ My Job.”

items.q: When and where was T.I.’s “24’s” recorded?
items.a: “24’s” was recorded at Patchwerk Recording Studios in Atlanta on 12 March 2002, seventeen months before Trap Muzik was released. Engineer Ismel Ramos tracked the beat and T.I.’s first verse in Studio 995 over a six-hour session from 10:30am to 4:30pm. The session report records two details rarely written down: the date was paid cash, circled on the sheet, and the song was recorded over a two-inch tape reel belonging to The City Boyz. Tape cost money in 2002.

items.q: Did Kanye West produce for T.I. on Trap Muzik?
items.a: Yes — Kanye West produced two tracks on Trap Muzik, “Doin’ My Job” and “Let Me Tell You Something,” and Patchwerk’s session reports place him in the building for both. He is listed as producer of record on 29 and 30 April and 1 May 2003, in Studio 995 and Studio 9000. The 1 May sheet logs both of his album tracks on the same night; the April dates add “I Wanna Be Your Man” and beats written down only as “Kanye 1” through “Kanye 5,” with a note that all of Kanye’s material was backed up to DVD. The album’s other producers named on Patchwerk sheets are DJ Toomp, Jazze Pha, San ‘Chez’ Holmes and Nick ‘Fury’ Loftin.

items.q: When were “Rubber Band Man” and “Let’s Get Away” recorded?
items.a: Both singles were cut in a single sixteen-hour session at Patchwerk Recording Studios on 9 April 2003, from 2pm to 6am the following morning. Mark “Exit” Goodchild engineered in Studio 9000 with Cory Williams assisting and Jazze Pha producing. The session report logs it in three blocks: “Let’s Get Away” vocals until 6pm, “Rubber Band Man” vocals until midnight, then “Rubber Band Man” mixed until dawn. Leslie Brathwaite mixed “Let’s Get Away” three days later in an eighteen-hour session.

items.q: Are there live instruments on Trap Muzik?
items.a: Yes. Live trumpet, saxophone and trombone were recorded for Trap Muzik at Patchwerk Recording Studios on 9 March 2003, in an overnight session running 10pm to 6am. Engineer Steve Fisher cut the horns for “Be Easy” and “Look What I Got,” edited both, then tracked a beat for “Be Better Than Me.” Mike Davis assisted at ten dollars an hour.

items.what: Tracked the 24’s beat and first verse. Paid cash. Recorded over The City Boyz’ two-inch reel.
Tracked the beat for “My Air Forces” — still billed to Arista, 1am to 5:30am.
Thirty CDs dubbed off DAT for T.I. and Foxy Brown.
Listening session with DJ Toomp. The sprint starts here.
Beats tracked for Look What I Got and Be Easy, then vocals on Be Easy.
items.who: Steve Fisher · prod. DJ Toomp · 7 hrs

items.what: Live trumpet, sax and trombone for Be Easy and Look What I Got; beat for Be Better Than Me.
Twelve hours of vocals: Bezzle, Be Better Than Me, King of da Souf, and the title track.
Vocals on Jump Off and Bezzle — and the album is sequenced for the first time.
8Ball & MJG verses and the Jazze Pha hook tracked onto Bezzle.
Music and vocals for “I Can’t Quit”, plus clean edits.
Fourteen hours mixing T.I. vs T.I.P. and the title track Trap Muzik.
Sixteen hours: Let’s Get Away vocals, then Rubber Band Man vocals, then Rubber Band Man mixed by dawn.
items.who: Exit, Cory Williams · prod. Jazze Pha · 2pm–6am

items.what: Eighteen hours mixing Let’s Get Away.
DAT to CD dupes of the shortlist: Let’s Get Away, Rubberband Man, Look What I Got, Bezzle, Trap Music.
Music and vocals tracked for I Still Love You, produced by Fury.
Kanye West in the room: Doin’ My Job tracked, plus I Wanna Be Your Man and beats logged only as “Kanye 1” through “Kanye 5.” Everything backed up to DVD.
Doin’ My Job, Let Me Tell You Something and a Still Country remix, Kanye producing. They brought their own CDs.
Thirteen hours finishing the record: the Buster Card Skit, the Album Intro, the Roland Interlude, and MPC music added to Trap Music.
A new mix of Trap Muzik and an Xtacy reprint — one hour, 2am to 3am.
Clean edits of Rubber Band Man as the single climbs.

sections.body: Trap Muzik is the record that turned a place into a genre. Every producer credited on it — Toomp, Jazze Pha, Kanye West, Fury, Chez — signed a Patchwerk session report to make it.

note: Engineering credits shown are drawn directly from Patchwerk’s own session logs for this record; only Patchwerk’s documented contributions are listed here.
